analysis.investment_thesis: Puravankara is a debt-laden real estate developer where finance costs (₹555 Cr) now exceed operating income (₹291 Cr), making the business economically loss-making at the operating level after debt service. With D/E of 2.75, negative ROE, and only 2.7% revenue CAGR over nine years, this is the opposite of the steady compounder I seek.
key_strengths: Promoter holding at 75% — committed and skin in the game
Gross margins of 44% indicate underlying pricing power in its project portfolio
Revenue recovered to ₹2,185 Cr in FY24 showing cyclical demand exists
key_risks: Debt/Equity of 2.75 is nearly 10x my maximum threshold of 0.3 — borrowings ballooned from ₹2,670 Cr (2020) to ₹4,497 Cr (2025)
Finance costs of ₹555 Cr in FY25 consumed all operating income (₹291 Cr) and then some — debt is destroying the business
Net loss of ₹183 Cr in FY25 with FCF of -₹572 Cr signals a capital-hungry model with no self-funding ability
red_flags: D/E of 2.75 — an absolute disqualifier under any scenario for me
Finance costs grew at 9.6% CAGR while revenue grew only 2.7% — leverage is compounding faster than the business
Net profit has been deeply volatile: ₹129 Cr → loss → ₹148 Cr → ₹42 Cr → -₹183 Cr — no earnings predictability whatsoever
OCF flipped from +₹896 Cr (FY24) to -₹531 Cr (FY25) — cash generation is not reliable
Real estate sector with aggressive debt-funded expansion — exactly the business model I have always avoided
analysis.detailed_analysis:
I have spent my career building and investing in businesses that generate predictable cash, carry no debt, and compound quietly. Puravankara fails every single criterion I care about. The debt story alone ends the conversation: borrowings have gone from ₹2,670 Cr in FY20 to ₹4,497 Cr in FY25, and interest costs at ₹555 Cr now exceed operating income of ₹291 Cr. That means the underlying real estate operations, even in a good year, cannot service this debt — the company is running on borrowed time and borrowed money. Equity has shrunk from ₹2,042 Cr in FY22 to ₹1,619 Cr in FY25 as losses erode book value.

The revenue trajectory is equally uninspiring — ₹1,584 Cr in FY16 to ₹2,014 Cr in FY25 is a 2.7% CAGR over nine years, barely keeping pace with inflation. Real estate developers are cyclical, capital-intensive, and highly leveraged by nature — I have always stayed away from this sector for precisely these reasons. The forward P/E of 23x on a loss-making company implies the market is pricing in a recovery that the balance sheet fundamentals do not support. At DMart, I never borrowed to grow. A business that needs ₹4,500 Cr in debt to generate ₹2,000 Cr in revenue with negative free cash flow is not a business — it is a liability.
